extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary and scientific biography; scholars and general readers interested in 19th-century American letters and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Biographical and critical sketches of 19th-century figures (John Holmes; Thaddeus W. Harris) focusing on their writing style, anecdotal portraits, scientific methods, teaching, and editorial/compilation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admirable dramatic arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'altogether an admirable dramatic arrangement, in which a terrific combination of tragic elements (all that the supposed spectator can bear) suddenly culminates in wise resolution, unanimous action, and general happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective drama combines intense tragic elements but leads to a clear climax and a wise, harmonious resolution (e.g., the mob's rage reversing to repentance and the tyrant's return to power). The passage illustrates valuing structural buildup to a satisfying resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of puns and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: 'John Holmes's humor sometimes, however, took the form of puns, but always with an apology, while Lowell never spared anything but the apology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing puns or similar devices, temper them with self-awareness or apology to preserve character authenticity and avoid excess; contrast: unrestrained punning (without apology) becomes Lowell's manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay on one's own ground (local authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'he kept carefully on his own ground, — Old Cambridge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity arises from writing rooted in the author's own milieu; remaining within familiar local subject-matter yields faithful, characteristic details that other writers may not reproduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, graphic description of local customs and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended illustrative passages (e.g., folding pew seats, Commencement tents and procession, the cocked hats, Latin theses, and social behavior) that reconstruct the past in sensory detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, physical details and lively anecdote to recreate historical social life; small, specific observations (sounds, movements, costumes) give scenes immediacy and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive moral or social insight from quotidian detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Holmes draws 'a new and unexpected moral from the creation of the mosquito' — the torment of night becomes a social medium for binding people the next day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary, even comic or irritating, everyday elements as lenses to make broader social or moral observations; these small details can illuminate communal psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety as a organizing principle in natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Were I to be required to say, in one word, what is the system of Nature, I should say — Variety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize diversity and variety when conceptualizing or presenting natural history; treat multiplicity of forms as central to natural-system thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical and accurate habits (scientific rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author praises 'the methodical and accurate habits of Dr. Harris' and his painstaking, systematized manuscript work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific and scholarly work should be methodical, accurate, and well-organized; routine discipline and exactness are prerequisites for higher scientific output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and compilation produce precision ('Writing maketh an exact man')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Writing maketh an exact man.' The text links laborious preliminary compilation with intellectual exactness and drill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough written compilation, indexing, and documentation cultivate precision of thought; the drudgery of organizing sources is itself pedagogically and epistemically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive bibliographic indexing and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed example: 'a complete systematic index to the butterflies described by Godart and Latreille... every genus or species is noted, with authority, reference, and synonyms... rearranged alphabetically...' and many similar manuscript indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain meticulous indices with authoritative references and synonyms; create systematic, searchable documentation (alphabetical rearrangement, per-genus/species notes) as foundational tools for scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local scope and reliance on first-hand observation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I was determined not to undertake to describe any insects but those which I had before my own eyes.' Also: plan for 'a local fauna insectorrimy which should include only the species common in this vicinity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit taxonomic or descriptive works to personally observed specimens and/or a clearly delimited local fauna; prioritize empirical, first-hand evidence over secondhand descriptions to ensure reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt language and presentation to audience for popularization
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I have rewritten my introduction in plain and simple language, divested as much as possible of all hard words, and intend to add ... brief descriptions ...' aimed at children to make entomology popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To popularize specialist subjects (especially to youth), simplify vocabulary, avoid technical jargon, and include brief, accessible descriptions targeted to the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic assessment of resources and project scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated references to lack of books, funds, and assistance; 'I have nearly abandoned all hope of bringing it to a successful termination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before committing to large scholarly projects, assess available resources (literature, specimens, funding, collaborators); adjust scope or postpone ambitions if foundational resources are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper specimen curation and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of Say's collections arriving in 'deplorable condition, most of the pins having become loose, the labels detached, and the insects themselves without heads, antennae, and legs, or devoured by destructive larvae... ground to powder by the perilous shakings' of transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure careful mounting, secure labeling, pest control, and safe transport/storage of specimens; poor curation destroys scientific value and undermines comparative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hands-on, enthusiastic teaching to inspire students
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Harris's private entomology class: 'He handled so fondly his little insect-martyrs, that it was enough to make one love this study for life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ direct, tactile engagement with specimens and visible enthusiasm when teaching to spark lasting interest in students; small, affectionate gestures toward material can be pedagogically powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target youth to build popular interest in science
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The difficulties met with, at length led me to think of some means of making entomology popular, and I looked to the young as the proper subjects to begin with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus outreach and introductory materials on children and youth as a strategy to seed wider popular interest and, indirectly, gain support from parents and communities.
